performed_via_github_app.description:
# 🦉 What is GitGuardian?

GitGuardian Secrets Detection detects and fixes vulnerabilities in source code at every step of the software development lifecycle, covering 350+ types of secrets like API keys, database connection strings, private keys, certificates, and more. The platform’s policy engine enables security teams to monitor and enforce rules across their VCS, DevOps tools, and infrastructure-as-code configurations. Our automated remediation playbooks and collaboration features bring security and development teams together to resolve incidents fast and in full.

## 1. Scan your codebase for 350+ types of secrets
GitGuardian scans your GitHub repositories and raises alerts only for critical secrets, such as API keys or other credentials. At scale, GitGuardian’s detection algorithm has been battle-tested on over three years of activity in all public GitHub repositories – totaling over 1 billion scanned commits!

## 2. Quickly remediate your hard-coded secrets
If you ever experience a leak involving a credential, we have a complete remediation guide used by 100k+ developers each year. We’ll show you how to revoke the secret and remove it from your git history.

##  3. Prevent secrets from reaching GitHub
Install ggshield, the GitGuardian CLI, and add secrets detection to your local development workflow using pre-commit and pre-push git hooks integrations.

# 🙋‍♂️ FAQ

**What is your pricing?**
GitGuardian is free for teams under 25 developers and offers a 30-day trial for larger teams.

**How can I be sure that GitGuardian won’t raise too many false positives?**
We have scanned billions of commits, sent millions of alerts since 2018, and integrated each feedback to improve our algorithm. Our alerts currently receive 91% “true positive” feedback from developers.

**My repositories are private; why should I install automated secret detection?**
Imagine if there were a plain text file with all your credit card numbers inside, you wouldn’t put this file inside your company’s git repository. Secrets are just as sensitive and should be handled with special care.

**Is GitGuardian available to be installed on-premise?**
Yes, you can contact one of our security specialists to look over the possibility of installing GitGuardian on-premise on your repositories.

# ⚒️ Installation notes 

You should install GitGuardian directly through your [GitGuardian](https://dashboard.gitguardian.com/) workspace on the Integration settings page. 

So that you know, your GitHub organization or GitHub account can only be associated with a single GitGuardian workspace.

# 👋 Support

If you experience any difficulties or have any questions, please reach out to us by email ([support@gitguardian.com](mailto:support@gitguardian.com)).

Addressed all four review comments in bae6cee:

1. **🔴 Opt-out command syntax** — The env var now sits before `sh` in both [install.sh](install.sh) (header comment) and the docs Note, so the downstream shell actually reads it:
   ```bash
   curl -fsSL https://get.agent-vault.dev | AGENT_VAULT_NO_TELEMETRY=1 sh
   ```
2. **🟡 Missing telemetry Note in `docs/self-hosting/local.mdx`** — Mirrored the disclosure after both the install command and the upgrade command.
3. **🟡 `AGENT_VAULT_NO_TELEMETRY` missing from canonical env-var refs** — Added to [.env.example](.env.example), a new "Installer" subsection in [docs/self-hosting/environment-variables.mdx](docs/self-hosting/environment-variables.mdx), and a new "Installer" section at the bottom of [docs/reference/cli.mdx](docs/reference/cli.mdx). Each entry notes the variable is installer-only (not read by the server or CLI binary).
4. **🟣 Pre-existing `BACKUP_FILE` bug** — Both message sites now gate on `[ -n "$BACKUP_FILE" ]` so a reinstall over a binary-only install (no database file) no longer prints a blank path while claiming a backup was made.

Rebased onto latest main and addressed all three review comments (commit e7b637b):

1. **🔴 Basic-auth credential routing (Twilio/Jira)** — Catalogued basic-auth services carry a token that belongs in the password slot, not username. `applyPreset` now calls `setPassword(tpl.suggested_credential_key)` for `auth_type === "basic"` and leaves username for the operator to fill (AccountSID / email is user-specific, not something the catalog can supply). Inline WHY comment explains the asymmetry.
2. **🔴 "Custom (blank)" leaving prior preset values** — Factored a `resetFields()` helper and call it at the top of every `applyPreset` invocation, including the empty-id branch. Picking a preset and then switching back to Custom now fully clears host/description/auth/credentials/headers.
3. **🟡 Mid-form layout shift when catalog arrives late** — `ServiceModal` now snapshots `catalog` at mount via `useState(() => catalog)` so a fetch resolving mid-form doesn't toggle `showPresets` into view above fields the user is already editing.

Typecheck + `vite build` green. Force-pushed after the rebase.

Both review findings addressed in 774b734 — dropping the keyer change entirely.

- **Over-broad exemption** (server.go:847): correct — `handleRegister`, `handleVerify`, `handleResendVerification`, `handleForgotPassword`, and `handleResetPassword` have no in-handler IP bucket, so the keyer-level exemption silently disarmed them for loopback callers. The PR description's defense-in-depth claim was wrong for those routes.
- **XFF spoofing** (ratelimit/key.go): correct — checking the XFF-derived `clientIP` rather than the direct TCP peer means a misconfigured trusted proxy turns the exemption into a remote bypass.

The route unwrap on the four public static reads (`/v1/service-catalog`, `/v1/skills/cli`, `/v1/skills/http`, `/v1/mitm/ca.pem`) is sufficient on its own: `vault run` only calls `/v1/mitm/ca.pem`, and the dashboard only fetches the CA PEM. The keyer change turned out to be unnecessary belt-and-suspenders that introduced both vulnerabilities. Reverted along with `IPKeySkipLoopback` and the now-orphaned `ipkeyer_test.go`.

Final diff vs main is 10 insertions / 8 deletions in `server.go` — just the route-unwrap.

All three review findings addressed in f242fd1.

**1. Live-tail burst loss** ([handle_logs.go:129](internal/server/handle_logs.go#L129) + [sqlite.go](internal/store/sqlite.go))
Tail queries (\`After > 0\`) now use \`ORDER BY id ASC LIMIT\`, so a burst >page-size is consumed oldest-first and the cursor advances through all of it over consecutive polls with no gaps. Handler reverses the slice before responding so the newest-first API contract is preserved, and \`latestID\` is taken from the new highest id. Regression test in [sqlite_test.go](internal/store/sqlite_test.go) pins the invariant.

**2. FK-violation batch rollback** ([handle_proxy.go:129](internal/server/handle_proxy.go#L129))
Guarded \`s.logSink.Record()\` with \`logVaultID != ""\` so the five early-exit paths (missing host, invalid host, no session, vault_error) no longer enqueue unattributable rows that the FK constraint would reject and take down the whole 250ms batch. These events still go to slog — they just aren't persisted, which is semantically correct since they occur before vault resolution. The MITM forward path (forward.go:48) was already safe because \`scope.VaultID\` is resolved at CONNECT time.

**3. Live-tail stuck on empty vault** ([LogsView.tsx:85](web/src/components/LogsView.tsx#L85))
Replaced the numeric \`latestIdRef.current === 0\` guard with a separate \`initializedRef\` boolean. It's reset alongside \`latestIdRef\` in the filter \`useEffect\` and set to \`true\` once \`loadInitial\` completes. Opening the Logs tab on an empty vault now polls correctly and picks up the first request without a reload; filter changes that produce zero results no longer permanently disable live tail.

\`go test ./...\` and \`golangci-lint run ./...\` both green.

The platform’s policy engine enables security teams to monitor and enforce rules across their VCS, DevOps tools, and infrastructure-as-code configurations. Our automated remediation playbooks and collaboration features bring security and development teams together to resolve incidents fast and in full.

## 1. Scan your codebase for 350+ types of secrets
GitGuardian scans your GitHub repositories and raises alerts only for critical secrets, such as API keys or other credentials. At scale, GitGuardian’s detection algorithm has been battle-tested on over three years of activity in all public GitHub repositories – totaling over 1 billion scanned commits!

## 2. Quickly remediate your hard-coded secrets
If you ever experience a leak involving a credential, we have a complete remediation guide used by 100k+ developers each year. We’ll show you how to revoke the secret and remove it from your git history.

##  3. Prevent secrets from reaching GitHub
Install ggshield, the GitGuardian CLI, and add secrets detection to your local development workflow using pre-commit and pre-push git hooks integrations.

# 🙋‍♂️ FAQ

**What is your pricing?**
GitGuardian is free for teams under 25 developers and offers a 30-day trial for larger teams.

**How can I be sure that GitGuardian won’t raise too many false positives?**
We have scanned billions of commits, sent millions of alerts since 2018, and integrated each feedback to improve our algorithm. Our alerts currently receive 91% “true positive” feedback from developers.

**My repositories are private; why should I install automated secret detection?**
Imagine if there were a plain text file with all your credit card numbers inside, you wouldn’t put this file inside your company’s git repository. Secrets are just as sensitive and should be handled with special care.

**Is GitGuardian available to be installed on-premise?**
Yes, you can contact one of our security specialists to look over the possibility of installing GitGuardian on-premise on your repositories.

# ⚒️ Installation notes 

You should install GitGuardian directly through your [GitGuardian](https://dashboard.gitguardian.com/) workspace on the Integration settings page. 

So that you know, your GitHub organization or GitHub account can only be associated with a single GitGuardian workspace.

# 👋 Support

If you experience any difficulties or have any questions, please reach out to us by email ([support@gitguardian.com](mailto:support@gitguardian.com)).

Rewriting git history is not a trivial act. You might completely break other contributing developers' workflow and you risk accidentally deleting legitimate data. :speech_balloon: **Discussion in Slack:** [#pr-review-agent-vault-113-feat-url-credential-substitutions-for-path-query-heade](https://infisical.slack.com/archives/C0AV42M6EP5)

_Posted by Review Police — reviews, comments, new commits, and CI failures will stream into this channel._

这个URL credential substitutions的设计很优雅，尤其是placeholder safety的几个约束：

> Length ≥ 4 characters, must contain `__` or a non-alphanumeric character

这种"最小惊讶原则"的做法是对的——与其让用户纠结"到底什么字符是安全的"，不如直接给出明确的规则。

**从一个Agent运营者的实战角度来看，我想提几个场景：**

1. **MCP Server连接** - 我们用OpenClaw的Agent连接各种MCP Server时，经常遇到API key需要嵌入URL的情况。目前大多数MCP实现都是直接把key写在配置文件里，这对多Agent环境来说是个安全噩梦。Agent Vault的proxy模式正好解决了这个问题。

2. **cron驱动的Agent** - 我们的多个AI Agent是cron定时触发的。如果每个Agent都持有独立凭证，凭证轮换（rotation）会变成运维灾难。Agent Vault的broker模式让所有Agent通过proxy访问，凭证集中管理+轮换，这个架构在1人公司×多Agent的场景下特别有价值。

3. **关于passthrough + substitutions的组合** - 这个设计很灵活，但要确保日志里不会泄露substitution后的完整URL。建议在broker层面对日志输出做redaction。

**一个小的改进建议：**

能否支持正则匹配的substitution？比如：
```yaml
services:
  - name: my-api
    url: "https://api.example.com/users/__user_id__"
    substitutions:
      - placeholder: "__user_id__"
        source: jwt_claims  # 从JWT token的claims中提取
```

这样Agent可以根据不同的请求上下文动态替换，而不是写死一个值。

——妙趣AI | https://miaoquai.com | 运营着5个AI Agent的1人公司

I would expect this integration to come out sometime end of next week or the week after since there are some user management / access control implications to think about when integrating the two.

Go give you more insight into how we're thinking thinking about AV: The idea is that folks should be able to use AV independently of a secrets manager but it would be a no-brainer to integrate it with one when running a more complete, fuller deployment. body: Closing as decided to go with a different direction closer to traditional MITM architecture with #133

FYI decided to resolve this issue by implementing something closer to the default behavior you'd expect from a MITM architecture.

Basically, we loosen the restriction on headers being passed through which you can read more about [here](https://docs.agent-vault.dev/learn/services#header-forwarding). Most headers will now pass through by default; the auth header (depending on the scheme that you configure will be injected at the proxy).

We will instead introduce more restrictive options in the future such that if you want to be more explicit about only letting select headers through then that will be possible through an allowlist. I think this default behavior should make sense for now because Agent Vault should follow a MITM architecture with credential brokering implemented on top of that.

Updated this PR with the two fixes I had made in `suhjohn/agent-vault`:

- `ec4520b` fixes MITM WebSocket 101 forwarding so the response does not accidentally include `Connection: close`.
- `d1e9f41` handles stale self-owned server PID files so container restarts do not get stuck when PID 1 matches persisted pidfile.

Validated locally with:

```sh
go test ./cmd ./internal/pidfile ./internal/mitm
```

Hey @siukwai ! going to trying to reproduce this. Quick couple questions:

1. Is the endpoint hermes is hitting http://ai/v1 or https://ai/v1? I see when you're inside of a tailnet things are already encrypted, but have you tried the https://ai.your-tailnet.ts.net endpoint?
2. Are hermes and Agent Vault running on the same machine for you?  Or are they on separate VM's / containers?

I'm inclined to believe that we want to set this to the https://ai.your-tailnet.ts.net (even though you're already inside the tailnet) because agent vault uses HTTPS CONNECT protocol to create a tunnel and intercept, modify headers, inject credentials, etc. 

If you've any other details that you think will be useful, let me know. Thanks!

body:
Addressing review feedback in 13dcff1:

**1. Vault mismatch detection** ([cmd/helpers.go](https://github.com/Infisical/agent-vault/blob/run-agent-mode/cmd/helpers.go)) — `validateEnvToken` now parses `/discover`'s response and rejects when `AGENT_VAULT_VAULT` names a different vault than the supplied scoped-session token's baked-in vault. The broker silently uses the session's vault and ignores `X-Vault` for scoped sessions, so without this check the child would see a misleading `AGENT_VAULT_VAULT` in its env. Two new sub-tests in `TestValidateEnvToken` cover the mismatch (rejected) and matching (passes) cases.

**2. Cross-links** — added the two pointers the plan called for:
- A "Deploy your agent in a container" card in the Next-steps section of [connect-custom-agent.mdx](https://github.com/Infisical/agent-vault/blob/run-agent-mode/docs/guides/connect-custom-agent.mdx).
- A disambiguation `<Note>` at the top of [container-isolation.mdx](https://github.com/Infisical/agent-vault/blob/run-agent-mode/docs/guides/container-isolation.mdx) clarifying that it's about sandboxing the dev-machine agent in a container — fundamentally different from shipping the agent *as* a container image.

**3. CHANGELOG** — skipped: this repo doesn't have a CHANGELOG file; the deprecation notice lives in the commit message + skill-file copy + env-var docs, which is the project convention.

Test status unchanged: `go test ./cmd/` green (incl. 4 sub-tests in `TestValidateEnvToken` now), `go vet` clean, `go build` clean.

```sh
AGENT_VAULT_ADDR=http://127.0.0.1:14321 ./agent-vault run --vault default --git -- \
```

```text
path=/dtetrac/eTracIntegrations/_git/etrac-as2-router/info/refs
```

```sh
AGENT_VAULT_ADDR=http://127.0.0.1:14321 ./agent-vault run --vault default --git -- \
  /opt/homebrew/bin/git ls-remote --heads \
```

Result:

```text
0690be9e2c266564a7a425e5b103120d7e661487 refs/heads/feature/vltrader-inbound-mailbox-delivery
569bb72d9549d1ba6ef57b7e01b0d2a580a8fbec refs/heads/main
```

Greptile Summary

 Adds an opt-out OpenClaw compatibility preload to `agent-vault run`: when the wrapped command is detected as OpenClaw, AV writes an embedded JS file to `~/.agent-vault/openclaw-compat.js` and injects it via `NODE_OPTIONS=--require=` into the child env. The preload patches axios in-process to fix two real bugs — axios v1.x's broken TLS-wrapped `HTTPS_PROXY` parsing and `@slack/web-api`'s body-token placement. - **`internal/openclawcompat/`**: new package embedding `preload.js` via `go:embed` and writing it atomically to disk; idempotent with stale-content recovery. - **`cmd/node_compat_flag.go`**: new `--node-compat=auto|on|off` cobra flag with `AGENT_VAULT_NODE_COMPAT` env fallback; auto-detection covers bare `openclaw` and `node`/`nodejs` wrapping an `/openclaw/`-pathed entrypoint, with conservative substring guards. - **`cmd/run.go`**: step 7.5 wires `EnsurePreload` + `appendNodeOptionsRequire` (tokenized idempotency); container-isolation path emits a warning when `--node-compat=on` is explicitly set since the preload is not bind-mounted into the container.

Confidence Score: 3/5

The proxy bypass concern in preload.js could cause openclaw's outbound axios requests to reach their upstreams without going through AV's audit or substitution layer on Node.js versions older than 22.7. The core Go machinery (flag parsing, atomic file write, env injection, detection logic) is well-tested and correct. The risk lives entirely in preload.js: axios.defaults.proxy = false disables axios's own HTTPS_PROXY reading, and the replacement mechanism (NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1) only wires axios's http-module adapter into Node's global proxy infrastructure starting in Node 22.7.0. If openclaw runs on Node 18 or 20 LTS, all axios HTTP requests silently bypass AV's MITM proxy, making credential substitution and audit logging inactive for those calls. internal/openclawcompat/preload.js — the attach() function's proxy disable interacts with the Node.js version of the openclaw deployment in a way that hasn't been addressed in the code or documentation.

Security Review

 - **Proxy bypass on Node < 22.7** (`internal/openclawcompat/preload.js`): `axios.defaults.proxy = false` disables axios's env-proxy integration. The intended fallback is `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1` (already injected by `BuildProxyEnv`), but this env var only affects Node's `http`/`https` module global agents from Node.js 22.7.0 onward. On Node 18 or 20 LTS, axios's http-module adapter makes direct connections, bypassing AV's MITM proxy entirely — outbound openclaw requests would be unaudited and credential substitution would not fire.

Important Files Changed

| Filename | Overview | |----------|----------| | internal/openclawcompat/preload.js | New embedded JS preload that patches axios in-process; the `proxy = false` fix may silently bypass AV's MITM proxy on Node < 22.7 where NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY doesn't affect the http/https module adapter axios uses. | | internal/openclawcompat/openclawcompat.go | New package: embeds preload.js and writes it atomically to ~/.agent-vault/openclaw-compat.js; idempotent across re-invocations, stale-content recovery correct, minor: deferred remove fires unnecessarily on the success path. | | cmd/node_compat_flag.go | New file implementing NodeCompatMode flag, nodeCompatEnabled detection logic, and appendNodeOptionsRequire; tokenized idempotency check is correct and well-tested. | | cmd/run.go | Integrates node-compat flag resolution (with AGENT_VAULT_NODE_COMPAT env fallback) and wires EnsurePreload + appendNodeOptionsRequire at step 7.5; container-mode warning is correct. | | cmd/node_compat_flag_test.go | Exhaustive test coverage for mode parser, nodeCompatEnabled (including substring-non-match guards), and appendNodeOptionsRequire; all cases look correct. | | internal/openclawcompat/openclawcompat_test.go | Five test cases covering canonical path write, idempotency, stale-content recovery, parent-dir permissions, and embed-content invariants; all look correct. |

Comments Outside Diff (2)

 1. `internal/openclawcompat/preload.js`, line 844-847 ([link](https://github.com/infisical/agent-vault/blob/ead1b3c41844bb54398a33a4d6cafb821d723a9a/internal/openclawcompat/preload.js#L844-L847)) **`proxy = false` bypasses AV's proxy on Node < 22.7** `axios.defaults.proxy = false` prevents axios from reading `HTTPS_PROXY` natively. The fallback relies on `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1` (already injected by `BuildProxyEnv`) routing requests through Node's built-in HTTP infrastructure. However, `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY` only affects the `http`/`https` module global agents starting in Node.js 22.7.0 — on Node 18 or 20 LTS, axios's http-module adapter makes direct connections, entirely bypassing AV's MITM proxy. Any openclaw axios request running on those Node versions would reach its upstream without going through AV's audit or substitution layer. 2. `internal/openclawcompat/openclawcompat.go`, line 586-593 ([link](https://github.com/infisical/agent-vault/blob/ead1b3c41844bb54398a33a4d6cafb821d723a9a/internal/openclawcompat/openclawcompat.go#L586-L593)) **Deferred remove always fires on the success path** `tmpName` is registered for best-effort cleanup via `defer os.Remove(tmpName)` before the rename. After `os.Rename(tmpName, path)` succeeds, `tmpName` no longer exists at that path, so the deferred `os.Remove` always gets a "no such file" error (silently discarded with `_ =`). A small sentinel (e.g., a `renamed` bool set to `true` after rename) would skip the redundant syscall on the happy path while still cleaning up on errors.

Pushed d5ad5e0 addressing CI + Greptile review.

**CI lint (gosec G306):** changed the stale-content fixture in `openclawcompat_test.go` from `0o644` to `0o600`. Test-only; the file just needs to look stale to the recovery path.

**Greptile P1 (Node 22.7 proxy bypass — security):** the concern is real. With `axios.defaults.proxy = false`, axios falls back to `https.globalAgent`, which only honors `HTTPS_PROXY` when `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY` is supported (Node ≥ 22.7). On Node 18/20 LTS, openclaw's axios calls would silently bypass the broker entirely.

Considered three fixes: (a) version check + fail-loud, (b) replace `proxy = false` with a parsed proxy-config object so axios uses its own proxy code path, (c) implement a TLS-tunnel `httpsAgent` in pure JS. Went with (a) — adds a 10-line check at the top of `preload.js` that throws a clear error if the runtime is too old. The other two paths depend on axios's own TLS-proxy code which has a history of regressions; I'd rather operators see a hard upgrade signal than chase silent fallthrough. Surfaced the requirement next to the `--node-compat` flag in `docs/reference/cli.mdx`, the `AGENT_VAULT_NODE_COMPAT` entry in `docs/self-hosting/environment-variables.mdx`, and `.env.example`.

**Greptile P2 (deferred `os.Remove` on success — cosmetic):** added a `renamed` sentinel so the deferred cleanup only fires when the rename never happened. Eliminates the unnecessary "no such file" syscall on the happy path.

Greptile Summary

 Adds a per-child loopback TLS terminator (`internal/proxybridge`) to let agents like Codex — whose HTTP libraries reject `https://`-scheme `HTTPS_PROXY` URLs — still route through Agent Vault's TLS-wrapped MITM proxy. When enabled, `syscall.Exec` is replaced by `os/exec.Cmd` with signal forwarding so the bridge goroutines outlive the exec call. - `internal/proxybridge/bridge.go`: new `Bridge` type that binds `127.0.0.1:0`, pins the MITM CA, and splices TCP↔TLS bidirectionally; test suite covers splice correctness, CA-trust failure, and loopback-only binding. - `cmd/run.go`: adds `--tls-bridge=auto|always|never` flag, a `knownAgents.needsTLSBridge` table entry for Codex, and `runBridgedChild` (fork+wait with SIGINT/SIGTERM drain); the bridge rewrites `HTTP(S)_PROXY` to the loopback address via the existing `BuildProxyEnv` helper.

Confidence Score: 3/5

The bridge introduces a cleartext credential leg on the host loopback in the default mode, and the parent process now has unhandled SIGHUP/SIGQUIT signals that the original exec path never had to deal with — both warrant fixes before shipping. The core bridge logic is well-structured and the test suite is thorough, but the cleartext Proxy-Authorization token exposed on the shared host loopback contradicts the stated security invariant in the default operating mode, and missing SIGHUP handling is a behavioral regression from the original syscall.Exec path. internal/proxybridge/bridge.go (cleartext loopback exposure) and cmd/run.go (signal handling, NO_PROXY conflict)

Security Review

 Adds two new substitution surfaces — `body` and `websocket` — so credentials can be injected into HTTP request bodies and WebSocket text frames, not just headers, paths, and query strings. Both surfaces are opt-in (not in `DefaultSubstitutionSurfaces`) and validated at service-creation time. - **Body substitution** (`"in": ["body"]`): buffers the already-materialized request body, applies placeholder replacement with content-type-aware encoding (URL-encode for `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, JSON-escape for `application/json`, identity otherwise), skips multipart and compressed bodies, and updates `Content-Length` via the `ContentLength` field. The fix from the previous review cycle (always reassigning `outReq.Body` regardless of whether a match was found) is present. - **WebSocket frame substitution** (`"in": ["websocket"]`): parses RFC 6455 frames on the client→server direction only; handles all three length encodings and the 7-bit→16-bit transition when substitution grows the payload; re-masks with `crypto/rand`; passes through binary, control, compressed, fragmented, and oversized (>1 MB) frames unmodified; strips `Sec-WebSocket-Extensions` from the upgrade handshake to prevent `permessage-deflate` compression making frames opaque.

Confidence Score: 5/5

Safe to merge. The new body and WebSocket substitution paths are well-guarded and do not introduce new attack vectors. Both new code paths are narrowly scoped to credential injection on operator-configured surfaces, have comprehensive unit tests including length-encoding boundary transitions and oversized-frame stream-through, and the previously flagged body-drain bug is correctly addressed. The only finding is a harmless redundant Header.Set call that Go's transport ignores. No files require special attention.

Important Files Changed

| Filename | Overview | |----------|----------| | internal/brokercore/substitution.go | New ApplyBodySubstitutions function with correct content-type-aware encoding (URL-encode for form, JSON-escape for JSON, identity for others), multipart skip, and proper empty/nil body guards. | | internal/mitm/forward.go | Wires ApplyBodySubstitutions before the existing substitution path; always reassigns outReq.Body to the fresh reader; only updates ContentLength when the body was modified. Minor: manual Content-Length header set is redundant (Go's transport ignores it in favour of ContentLength field). | | internal/mitm/websocket.go | Adds frame-level WebSocket substitution: correctly handles 7/16/64-bit length encodings, MSB overflow guard, unmask/re-mask with crypto/rand, 1 MB payload cap, fast-path for no-change frames, and clean pass-through for binary/control/fragmented/compressed frames. | | internal/brokercore/substitution_test.go | 12 body-substitution unit tests covering form-encoding, JSON escaping, multipart skip, charset params, nil/empty body, no-match, and surface scoping. | | internal/mitm/websocket_test.go | New test file: 8 tests covering text substitution, binary/ping/close pass-through, length-encoding transition (7-bit to 16-bit), oversized frame stream-through, and filterWebSocketSubs helper. | | internal/broker/broker.go | Adds 'body' and 'websocket' to SubstitutionSurfaces and removes the former 'body is reserved' rejection guard. | | sdks/sdk-typescript/src/resources/services.ts | SubstitutionSurface type extended with 'body' and 'websocket' to match the new backend surfaces. | | web/src/components/ProposalPreview.tsx | SUBSTITUTION_SURFACES constant updated to include 'body' and 'websocket'; DEFAULT_SUBSTITUTION_SURFACES unchanged (opt-in only). | Reviews (2): Last reviewed commit: ["fix: always update outReq.Body after App..."](https://github.com/infisical/agent-vault/commit/8629721bc95fd1731d47a5a9ffaa899d60388f50) | [Re-trigger Greptile](https://app.greptile.com/api/retrigger?id=34958922)

Greptile Summary

 Fixes a bug where every CONNECT/forward-proxy request — even those with valid credentials — consumed from the `TierAuth` rate-limit budget, causing remote agents to receive 429s after ~10 connections. The fix introduces a read-only `Check()` peek that gates on whether the budget is already exhausted, and only records an event (`Allow()`) when authentication actually fails. - **`sliding.go` / `registry.go`**: Adds `check()` / `Check()` — a read-only budget peek that prunes expired timestamps and tests the limit without writing a new event. - **`connect.go` / `forward.go`**: Replaces the `Allow` pre-gate with `Check`, adds `recordAuthFailure()` called only on auth-failure branches; successful auth skips `TierAuth` entirely. - **Docs / UI**: Updates `TierAuth` descriptions and removes the now-unnecessary \"disable rate limiting\" workaround from the Hermes-on-VPS guide.

Confidence Score: 5/5

Safe to merge. The check-then-record pattern is correct, well-tested, and the intentional TOCTOU trade-off is already acknowledged and covered by the test suite. The change is narrowly scoped: swapping a recording call for a peek in two handler entry points and routing recording to the failure path. The new check() implementation correctly avoids appending a timestamp while still pruning expired entries and enforcing the budget. Five new integration tests and three unit tests for Check() cover the core invariants. No pre-existing auth, session, or forwarding logic was modified. No files require special attention.

Important Files Changed

| Filename | Overview | |----------|----------| | internal/ratelimit/sliding.go | Adds check() — a sliding-window peek that prunes expired entries and tests the budget without recording a new event. Exclusive mutex is appropriate since eviction writes to the map. | | internal/ratelimit/registry.go | Adds Registry.Check() using r.mu.RLock() to protect the pointer lookup and delegating to slidingWindow.check(). Other tier types correctly fail open. | | internal/mitm/connect.go | Switches CONNECT pre-gate from Allow to Check, adds recordAuthFailure() on ParseProxyAuth and ResolveForProxy failures only. Greptile Summary

 This PR makes MITM proxy body-size caps configurable: response bodies are now unlimited by default (streamed with a 32 KB buffer, no OOM risk), and request bodies default to 1 GiB (up from 64 MB), fixing `git clone` and `git push` failures for large repositories. Request bodies with a known `Content-Length` and no body substitutions are now streamed directly to the upstream instead of being fully buffered in RAM. - **Response limit**: operators set `--max-response-bytes` / `AGENT_VAULT_MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES`; known-oversize returns 502, chunked oversize aborts the connection via `http.ErrAbortHandler` with a structured `slog.Warn` on both paths. - **Request limit**: operators set `--max-request-bytes` / `AGENT_VAULT_MAX_REQUEST_BYTES`; known-length bodies exceeding the limit get an immediate 413; bodies requiring RAM materialization (chunked or body-substitution) are still capped at a hard 64 MB `MaxMaterializeBytes`. - **Streaming optimization**: `HasBodySubstitutions` decides at runtime whether to stream (common path: git, file uploads) or materialize (body substitutions); `ApplyBodySubstitutions` has a matching early-exit when no body subs are present, confirming the streaming path is safe.

Confidence Score: 5/5

Safe to merge; the core streaming logic is correct, ApplyBodySubstitutions returns immediately when no body subs exist, and all three startup paths (foreground, detached child, spawned child) consistently thread the new limits through. The change is well-tested (7 new integration tests covering 502 rejection, mid-stream abort, exact-fit pass-through, unlimited default, and configurable caps), the ApplyBodySubstitutions early-exit was verified to make the streaming path safe, and no new request-routing or host-validation code was introduced. The two findings are observability and documentation gaps that do not affect correctness for the primary use cases. No files require special attention beyond the noted documentation gap in the CLI/env-var docs for chunked request behavior.

The motivation is to stop agents from proactively running `discover` before every API call, making the proxy feel transparent. - **Code changes** (`server.go`, `handle_services.go`, `cmd/server.go`, `cmd/run.go`): `SetSkills` signature narrowed to a single `cli string` parameter; `handleSkillHTTP` handler and its mux route deleted; both call-sites in the detached-child and main server paths updated consistently. All changes are correct and complete. - **Skill rewrite** (`cmd/skill_cli.md`): Agents now make requests directly and create proposals only on 401/403 failures. The 10-minute polling ceiling is preserved. The 429 rate-limit handling from the old skills was not carried over, and the always-visible description has a minor inconsistency for `service_disabled` 403s.

Confidence Score: 5/5

The Go code changes are minimal and mechanically correct — a signature narrowing, a route deletion, two call-site updates, and a comment refresh. No logic paths were altered. All changed Go files touch either the skill-serving plumbing (route/handler deletion, struct field removal) or doc comments. The edits are consistent across both server startup paths, the brokercore help-link string, and tests. No auth flows, credential handling, or proxy logic were touched. body: @mvanhorn can you get the merge conflict resolved?

Hey @DoradoPR, thanks for evaluating Agent Vault! Here's where things stand on the items you flagged:

**Build provenance (#138) and Docker image signing (#139)** — Both reviewed. Waiting on the author to resolve a merge conflict on #138 and address minor feedback on #139. These are moving forward.

**DNSSEC on `agent-vault.dev`** — Now enabled.

**Installer integrity verification (item 10)** — We've thought about this and we're not convinced it adds meaningful security. At every level, either the threat is already mitigated or in-script verification doesn't help:

- **Network attacks** → blocked by HTTPS + DNSSEC
- **Source compromised** → if an attacker controls `install.sh`, they just remove the verification. You can't verify from inside a compromised script.
- **Release assets swapped** → blocked by Immutable Releases (enabled)
- **GitHub account or CI compromised** → the build is legitimately signed, so all verification passes anyway
- **Corrupted download** → `tar xzf` already fails on bad archives

It also introduces tool dependencies (`cosign` / `gh`) that most machines don't have, which works against the goal of a simple install path.

Happy to discuss further if you see a gap in this reasoning.

@SamMousa So, you're thinking of approvals on the HTTP requests? Need to think about how this can be done in a manageable way.

What do you mean by SSH agent? Is the agent the one creating the approval requests and also approving it on interactive user input?

Yes, approvals on API requests. Ssh agents allow you to add a key, with a confirm option. So the agent will always require user confirmation to the agent that it is okay to use the key. Just look for ssh agent confirm online to see what I mean.

@greptile review again based on the latest changes

Greptile Summary

 This PR hardens CI and the Node SDK release workflow against supply-chain attacks by adding `--ignore-scripts` to all `npm ci` invocations, preventing transitive dependency lifecycle scripts from executing during installs. The frontend build recovers the one known install-script dependency (`esbuild`) with an explicit `npm rebuild esbuild` before `vite build`. - `ci.yml` frontend job: `npm ci --ignore-scripts && npm rebuild esbuild && npm run build` — correctly isolated. - `ci.yml` sdk-ts job and `release-node-sdk.yml`: `npm ci --ignore-scripts` added, but no `npm rebuild esbuild` step, despite both jobs running `tsup` (an esbuild-based bundler) and `vitest` (which also uses esbuild). The SDK's `prepublishOnly` script runs `tsup` implicitly during `npm publish`, introducing the same esbuild-binary dependency that the frontend job explicitly handles.

Confidence Score: 4/5

Safe to merge with low risk; the hardening intent is correct and the frontend change is properly handled, but the SDK CI and release jobs may silently fail if esbuild's binary setup requires its install script. The frontend job is correctly hardened. The SDK CI job and release workflow are inconsistent — both run tsup (and vitest), which depend on esbuild, without the npm rebuild esbuild step that the frontend job uses to restore esbuild's binary after --ignore-scripts. Whether this causes failures depends on the exact esbuild version and npm behaviour on the runner, but the inconsistency is a real gap that could surface as a broken SDK build or publish. .github/workflows/ci.yml (sdk-ts job) and .github/workflows/release-node-sdk.yml both need a npm rebuild esbuild step added after npm ci --ignore-scripts to match the pattern used in the frontend-build job.

Important Files Changed

| Filename | Overview | |----------|----------| | .github/workflows/ci.yml | Adds --ignore-scripts to npm ci in frontend-build and sdk-ts jobs; frontend correctly adds npm rebuild esbuild, but sdk-ts job is missing the same step despite using tsup (esbuild-based) | | .github/workflows/release-node-sdk.yml | Adds --ignore-scripts to npm ci; npm publish will still trigger prepublishOnly (tsup build via esbuild) without a prior npm rebuild esbuild, inconsistent with the frontend approach |

Comments Outside Diff (2)

 1. `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, line 166-176 ([link](https://github.com/infisical/agent-vault/blob/2266a5c8c45da927c5bb961692035ef476634eec/.github/workflows/ci.yml#L166-L176)) **Missing `npm rebuild esbuild` before SDK build steps** The `sdk-ts` job adds `--ignore-scripts` but never calls `npm rebuild esbuild`. The SDK's build script (`tsup`) and test runner (`vitest`) both rely on esbuild for bundling and transformation. The frontend job explicitly adds `npm rebuild esbuild` for exactly this reason. If esbuild's postinstall is needed to locate or validate its binary on the runner, `npm run build` and `npm test` will silently break here. The inconsistency between the two jobs (frontend rebuilds esbuild, SDK does not) suggests this step may have been overlooked. 2. `.github/workflows/release-node-sdk.yml`, line 36-43 ([link](https://github.com/infisical/agent-vault/blob/2266a5c8c45da927c5bb961692035ef476634eec/.github/workflows/release-node-sdk.yml#L36-L43)) **`prepublishOnly` build uses tsup/esbuild with no prior `npm rebuild esbuild`** After `npm ci --ignore-scripts`, `npm publish` triggers `prepublishOnly: npm run build` (declared in `package.json`), which runs `tsup` — an esbuild-based bundler. If esbuild's native binary is not properly initialised (the same concern addressed by `npm rebuild esbuild` in the frontend job), the publish step's implicit build will fail. Adding `npm rebuild esbuild` (or an explicit `npm run build`) before `npm publish` would make this consistent with how the frontend job handles the same dependency.

Greptile Summary

 This PR adds first-class support for mounting the Agent Vault UI and `/v1` API under a configurable URL path prefix (`--ui-base-path` / `AGENT_VAULT_UI_BASE_PATH`), solving the longstanding reverse-proxy pain of requiring content-rewriting proxies. The mechanism is clean: Vite builds with relative asset URLs, the Go server rewrites only the unhashed `index.html`'s `` at startup, and the SPA derives its router basepath and API prefix from that tag at runtime. - `NormalizeBasePath` in `basepath.go` validates the operator-supplied prefix; `injectBasePath` rewrites the single `index.html` placeholder; the outer mux strips the prefix before delegating to the existing inner mux, preserving all existing route handling while keeping `/health` at the domain root. - `apiFetch` in `api.ts` prepends `basePath` to all root-relative calls, and the remaining raw `fetch()` calls in `VaultLayout` and `Navbar` are migrated to go through it. - A drive-by bug fix correctly registers `/fonts/` and `/favicon.*` routes that previously returned 404 even at the domain root.

Confidence Score: 4/5

Safe to merge after addressing the missing HTML-unsafe character rejection in NormalizeBasePath; all other paths are well-tested. The NormalizeBasePath validator does not reject double-quote, less-than, or greater-than characters, and injectBasePath places the value directly into an HTML attribute string. A quote character would silently break the injected base tag and cause the SPA to fail loading under the prefix. The rest of the change is correct and well-covered by tests. internal/server/basepath.go — the character allowlist in NormalizeBasePath should be extended to cover HTML-attribute-unsafe characters.

Security Review

 - **Base-tag injection via unvalidated characters**: `NormalizeBasePath` does not reject `\"` (double-quote), `<`, or `>`. The injected value is placed directly into an HTML attribute (``). A path containing `\"` would break the attribute and silently redirect all SPA assets to the wrong path. The prefix is operator-supplied config, but defense-in-depth warrants rejecting these characters.

Greptile Summary

 This PR adds HashiCorp Vault as a third read-only external credential store, mirroring the existing Infisical integration. It introduces `internal/hashicorp` (auth detection, vault/api client, periodic syncer), a SQLite migration to widen the `kind` CHECK constraint, server wiring for a second sync worker with correct DEK-drain ordering on shutdown, handler dispatch by store kind, CLI flags, and web form fields. - **`internal/hashicorp`**: New package with AppRole/Token auth detection, `FetchSecrets` for KV v1+v2, and a `Syncer` that mirrors the Infisical syncer's tick/in-flight/backoff pattern. Upstream error bodies are scrubbed from API responses; invalid-key names are gated to admin/owner callers. - **Server/store**: Migration 050 rebuilds `vault_credential_stores` with `'hashicorp'` added to the `kind` CHECK; `Start()` correctly drains both external-store syncers before wiping the DEK; `createHashicorpVault` reuses the same owner-gated, probe-then-commit flow as `createInfisicalVault`. - **CLI/docs**: New `--credential-store=hashicorp` flags with matching validation and documentation.

Confidence Score: 4/5

Safe to merge with minor follow-up recommended on path validation and the login-goroutine context. The core feature — auth-method detection, KV fetch, encrypted snapshot storage, syncer lifecycle, DEK-drain ordering, and owner-only gating — is implemented correctly and mirrors the proven Infisical path. The two areas worth attention before the next iteration are: the `mount`/`secret_path` fields accept `../` and Vault system-path prefixes without rejection (letting an owner probe beyond the intended KV namespace), and the login goroutine in `attachHashicorpIfConfigured` runs against `context.Background()` so it outlives its 10 s deadline. Neither causes a breach or data corruption in the normal path, but both are worth tightening. `internal/hashicorp/config.go` (path validation gap) and `cmd/server.go` (login goroutine context).

Security Review

 - **Path-level access not scoped to KV namespace** (`internal/hashicorp/config.go`): `VaultConfig.Validate()` does not reject `../` traversal sequences or Vault system prefixes (e.g. `sys/`) in `mount` or `secret_path`. An instance owner can aim the broker at arbitrary paths on the configured Vault server. The host is fixed by the operator-set `VAULT_ADDR`, so this is not a host-level SSRF, but path-scope is broader than the intended KV read surface. - No new unauthenticated endpoints; external-store creation is correctly gated to the instance owner. Upstream error bodies are scrubbed before API responses. `VAULT_TOKEN`/`VAULT_ROLE_ID`/`VAULT_SECRET_ID` are read from env only and never logged or returned.

Important Files Changed

| Filename | Overview | |----------|----------| | internal/hashicorp/auth.go | New file: auth-method detection (AppRole vs Token). Logic is correct; `DetectAuthMethod` has a vestigial error return that is always nil. | | internal/hashicorp/client.go | New file: vault/api client wrapper and `FetchSecrets`. Token lookup-self probe on startup is good. `stringValue` coercion is thorough. | | internal/hashicorp/config.go | New file: VaultConfig parsing and validation. `Validate()` lacks path traversal checks on `mount`/`secret_path`; `mount` trimming is asymmetric with `secret_path`. | | internal/hashicorp/sync.go | New file: periodic and manual syncer. In-flight guard, backoff-via-bump, DEK-drain on shutdown all correctly implemented. ErrInvalidKey surfacing to admin/owner only is well-gated. | | cmd/server.go | Adds `attachHashicorpIfConfigured`. Login goroutine receives `context.Background()` so it runs past the 10s deadline; a context-with-timeout should be passed instead. | | internal/server/handle_vaults.go | Adds `createHashicorpVault` and dispatches sync/list by kind. Upstream error scrubbing, config/error redaction for non-admin viewers, and owner gate all look correct. | | internal/server/server.go | Adds hashicorp client/syncer fields and startup wiring. DEK-wipe drain correctly waits on both syncers before zeroing encKey. | | internal/store/migrations/050_hashicorp_credential_store.sql | SQLite table-rebuild migration to widen the `kind` CHECK constraint. Correct pattern for SQLite; foreign keys turned off and back on; existing rows preserved. | | cmd/vaults.go | Adds `hashicorp` case to `vaultCreateCmd` and `printCredentialStore`. Validation matches server-side constraints. |

Comments Outside Diff (1)

 1. `cmd/server.go`, line 78-92 ([link](https://github.com/infisical/agent-vault/blob/ef794ed25bbc21a1d3c12e20ddafd829dac084d5/cmd/server.go#L78-L92)) **Login goroutine not bounded by the 10s deadline** `hashicorp.NewClient` receives `context.Background()`, so the `WriteWithContext`/`LookupSelfWithContext` calls inside `login()` are never cancelled when the `time.After(10 * time.Second)` case fires. If the Vault server is reachable but slow, the goroutine can block for the full TCP keep-alive or OS connection timeout (up to several minutes), silently holding the vault/api HTTP connection pool open. Because the channel is buffered the goroutine eventually completes and its result is discarded — but the delay and wasted resources are avoidable. Passing a `context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)` into the goroutine instead would cancel the underlying RPC when the outer deadline fires.

Greptile Summary

 This PR separates agent revoke (soft-delete, `DELETE /v1/agents/{name}`) from agent delete (hard-delete, `POST /v1/agents/{name}/delete`), adds reactivation-by-rotation for revoked agents, and wires all three actions into a new frontend dropdown per agent row. - `DeleteAgent` removes sessions, vault grants, and the agents row in a single transaction; the CLI gains a distinct `agent delete` command while the old `delete` is renamed to `revoke`. - `RotateAgentToken` now unconditionally sets `status='active'` so rotating a revoked agent brings it back; the frontend rotate modal displays the new token once with a copy button. - The delete and revoke confirmation modals require typed-name confirmation before executing the irreversible action.

Confidence Score: 4/5

Safe to merge with one authorization fix: a non-owner member can currently undo an owner's revocation by rotating the agent's token. The store, CLI, and frontend changes are all correct. The gap is in handleAgentRotate: removing the revoked-status guard without a compensating check allows a non-owner creator to receive a fresh active token for an agent an owner deliberately revoked. internal/server/handle_agents.go — handleAgentRotate needs a guard preventing non-owners from rotating a revoked agent.

Security Review

 - **Privilege escalation via token rotation** (`internal/server/handle_agents.go`, `handleAgentRotate`): removing the `Status != \"active\"` guard without a compensating check means a non-owner member who created an agent can call the rotate endpoint to reactivate an agent that an instance owner explicitly revoked, issuing a new live token and silently undoing the administrative action.

Important Files Changed

| Filename | Overview | |----------|----------| | internal/server/handle_agents.go | Adds handleAgentDelete (auth logic consistent with revoke/rotate) and removes the revoked-status guard from handleAgentRotate, which lets a non-owner agent creator reactivate an owner-revoked agent. | | internal/store/sqlite.go | Adds DeleteAgent (sessions + vault_grants + agents row in one transaction) and updates RotateAgentToken to unconditionally set status='active'. Both look correct. | | internal/server/server_test.go | Adds TestAgentDelete and TestAgentRotate_ReactivatesRevokedAgent; mock RotateAgentToken correctly updates agent state via pointer. | | web/src/pages/home/AllAgentsTab.tsx | Adds rotate token modal (shows new token once, copy button), revoke/delete confirmation modals; RowActions now shows actions for revoked agents. Logic and state management look correct. | | cmd/agent.go | Renames old delete command to revoke, adds new delete command POSTing to /v1/agents/{name}/delete. Both commands use url.PathEscape correctly. | | cmd/cmd_test.go | Updates subcommand registration test to expect both revoke and delete. Trivial change, looks correct. | | internal/store/store.go | Adds DeleteAgent to the Store interface. No issues. | | internal/server/server.go | Registers POST /v1/agents/{name}/delete with limitBody and the standard auth middleware chain. No issues. | | docs/reference/cli.mdx | Adds revoke accordion, updates delete description, notes that rotating a revoked agent reactivates it. Documentation is accurate. |

Comments Outside Diff (1)

 1. `internal/server/handle_agents.go`, line 344-349 ([link](https://github.com/infisical/agent-vault/blob/a8ed97fcbaef312bf36b1782dab36c1536ad2ace/internal/server/handle_agents.go#L344-L349)) **Non-owner creator can undo an owner's revocation via token rotation** The previous guard `if agent.Status != "active" { return 409 }` was removed to enable reactivation-by-rotation. However the remaining authorization only blocks non-owners from managing agents they didn't create — it doesn't prevent a non-owner member who *did* create an agent from rotating (and thereby reactivating) one that an instance owner deliberately revoked. Concrete scenario: owner revokes `agent-foo` (created by member Alice) as a security response → Alice calls `POST /v1/agents/agent-foo/rotate` → passes both guards (agent is not owner-role, Alice is the creator) → `RotateAgentToken` sets `status='active'` unconditionally → owner's revocation is silently undone and a new live token is issued. Consider adding a check that blocks non-owners from rotating a revoked agent: if the caller is not an owner and the agent's current status is `"revoked"`, return `403 Forbidden` instead of proceeding.

Greptile Summary

 This PR ships the backend half of credential-store switching: a new `PATCH /v1/vaults/{name}/credential-store` endpoint, `SetVaultExternalStore` / `DeleteVaultCredentialStore` store methods, a `vault credential-store set` CLI command with typed confirmation, and updated docs. There is one security-relevant permission inconsistency introduced by the new endpoint. - **New endpoint `PATCH /v1/vaults/{name}/credential-store`** allows vault admins or instance owners to connect a vault to Infisical (overwriting built-in credentials with a fresh snapshot) or disconnect it (stopping polling while keeping synced secrets as built-in credentials). - **Store layer** adds `SetVaultExternalStore` (upsert + atomic credential replace in one transaction) and `DeleteVaultCredentialStore` (idempotent row delete), both extracting the shared `replaceCredentialsTx` helper. - **Permission inconsistency**: the Infisical connect path is accessible to vault admins, while `handleVaultCreate` gates external-store creation as owner-only specifically to prevent non-owners from using the server's Infisical machine identity to access upstream secrets.

Confidence Score: 3/5

Not safe to merge without resolving the permission inconsistency on the Infisical connect path. The Infisical connect branch of the new PATCH endpoint is accessible to vault admins, directly contradicting the deliberate owner-only gate in the vault-create path. The create handler's own comment names the threat, and the PATCH endpoint lets a non-owner instance member reproduce the blocked flow by creating a builtin vault first. Store layer and CLI changes are solid; the concern is isolated to the auth check on one branch of the new handler. internal/server/handle_vaults.go — specifically the CredentialStoreInfisical branch of handleVaultCredentialStorePatch.

Security Review

 - **Privilege escalation via credential-store switch** (`internal/server/handle_vaults.go`): The `PATCH /v1/vaults/{name}/credential-store` Infisical connect path is gated by `resolveVaultForAdminOrOwner` (vault admin allowed), while `handleVaultCreate` gates external-store creation as owner-only. Any instance member can create a builtin vault, gain vault admin, then PATCH it to Infisical with an arbitrary `project_id`/`environment`/`secret_path`, using the server's machine identity to fetch secrets from any Infisical project the server can reach.

Important Files Changed

| Filename | Overview | |----------|----------| | internal/server/handle_vaults.go | Adds handleVaultCredentialStorePatch and refactors prepareInfisicalSnapshot; the Infisical connect branch is accessible to vault admins, bypassing the owner-only guard that exists on the create path. | | internal/store/sqlite.go | Adds SetVaultExternalStore (upsert + credential replace in one transaction) and DeleteVaultCredentialStore (idempotent row delete); replaceCredentialsTx helper correctly extracted; minor syncer race on disconnect. | | cmd/vaults.go | Adds vaultCredentialStoreSetCmd with typed confirmation and directional warnings; refactors Infisical flag parsing into shared helper; correct URL path-escaping and payload structure. | | cmd/cmd_test.go | Tests for new credential-store set subcommand registration and flag presence; nil dereference risk if "set" subcommand is absent due to non-fatal t.Errorf before using setCmd. | | internal/server/server.go | Registers new PATCH /v1/vaults/{name}/credential-store route and extends Store interface; correct middleware chain. | | internal/server/server_test.go | Adds mock implementations and four handler tests covering builtin switch, forbidden member, invalid kind, and no-Infisical-client cases. | | internal/store/sqlite_test.go | New tests cover overwrite-on-connect, upsert idempotency, and keep-credentials-on-disconnect; thorough assertions. | | internal/store/store.go | Adds SetVaultExternalStoreParams and extends the Store interface; clean and consistent with existing patterns. | | docs/learn/credential-stores.mdx | Documents switching semantics, CLI examples, and HTTP reference; corrects poll-interval update description. | | docs/reference/cli.mdx | Adds credential-store set accordion with flag table; updates show description to reference new command. |

Comments Outside Diff (2)

 1. `cmd/cmd_test.go`, line 29-35 ([link](https://github.com/infisical/agent-vault/blob/8209b77bbe6b7da165617f0cde1dccffa7755ca0/cmd/cmd_test.go#L29-L35)) **Nil dereference if "set" subcommand is absent** The loop above uses `t.Errorf` (non-fatal) to flag missing subcommands, so execution continues even if "set" is not registered. `findSubcommand(csCmd, "set")` then returns nil, and the unconditional `setCmd.Flags().Lookup(...)` call panics rather than producing a clean test-failure message. Using `t.Fatalf` for the "set" check, or adding `if setCmd == nil { t.Fatal(...) }` before the flag loop, would prevent the panic. 2. `internal/store/sqlite.go`, line 769-779 ([link](https://github.com/infisical/agent-vault/blob/8209b77bbe6b7da165617f0cde1dccffa7755ca0/internal/store/sqlite.go#L769-L779)) **In-flight syncer can overwrite "kept" credentials after disconnect** `DeleteVaultCredentialStore` is not transactional with the syncer loop. If a sync goroutine has already fetched the vault's ID from `ListVaultCredentialStores` and is mid-flight, it will still call `ReplaceVaultCredentials` after the row is deleted, silently overwriting the credentials the disconnect is meant to preserve. The subsequent `UpdateVaultCredentialStoreHealth` call also silently fails (no row). The result is that credentials may be swapped for a slightly different Infisical snapshot and then frozen — a minor semantic divergence from the documented "keeps the last synced secrets."

Greptile Summary

 This PR adds a complete, runnable TypeScript Slack agent template under `examples/slack-agent-template` — including a Bolt Socket Mode bot, Claude Agent SDK integration with MCP-style local tools, optional email allowlist, Agent Vault Docker deployment, and accompanying docs. - **Slack bot** (`src/slack.ts`): handles `app_mention` and DM events, fetches thread transcripts for context, posts progress updates, and chunks long responses within Slack's character limit. - **Two starter tools**: `echo` (placeholder) and `example_api_get` (constrained read-only HTTP GET with Zod validation and path normalization). - **Access control** (`src/access.ts`): optional `AGENT_ALLOWLIST` env var gates users by Slack email; well-tested and safe-by-default when unconfigured.

Confidence Score: 3/5

The agent template is well-structured and thoughtfully designed, but the example HTTP tool follows redirects without restriction, which could expose internal services when the template is deployed in cloud environments. The fetch call in `example-api.ts` has no redirect guard. In a cloud deployment where the configured API endpoint issues a `3xx` redirect to an internal service (e.g., the instance metadata API), Node's `fetch` follows it and hands the response back to the AI — and from there into the Slack thread. The path is AI-controlled and can be shaped by Slack user prompts, making this a real threat surface rather than a theoretical one. The fix is a single-line addition (`redirect: "error"`), but without it the example ships a redirect-based SSRF vector that template consumers are unlikely to add themselves. examples/slack-agent-template/src/tools/example-api.ts — the fetch call needs `redirect: "error"`; also review the base-URL path-override behavior documented in the test.

Greptile Summary

 This PR introduces a Helm chart for Agent Vault under `charts/agent-vault`, with documentation updates in the root README and `docs/installation.mdx`. The chart covers SQLite-by-default with optional PostgreSQL, secret wiring via `secretEnv` or `existingSecret`, optional Ingress for the management UI, and intentionally keeps the MITM proxy port off the public Ingress. - **Deployment template** has two functional issues: every key projected from `existingSecret` is marked `optional: true`, which silently swallows a missing `AGENT_VAULT_MASTER_PASSWORD` and lets the pod start unconfigured; and there is no Helm `fail` guard preventing `replicaCount > 1` when `persistence.enabled: true`, a combination that causes PVC scheduling failures and SQLite corruption. - **Default proxy network policy** is unrestricted — `AGENT_VAULT_NETWORK_ALLOWLIST` is commented out, leaving any pod in the cluster able to route arbitrary requests through the MITM proxy to internal endpoints including cloud metadata services. - **Ingress template** is missing a `| quote` on the TLS `secretName` field, inconsistent with how `host` is handled.

Confidence Score: 3/5

The chart should not be merged as-is for production use; the silent-optional-secret and replica+PVC issues can both result in broken or misconfigured deployments with no clear diagnostic signal. Two functional bugs in the deployment template — silent swallowing of a missing master-password key, and an unchecked replica/PVC combination that corrupts SQLite — combine to make the chart unreliable in realistic operator error scenarios. The unrestricted proxy SSRF is an additional concern in shared clusters. The rest of the chart (security context, service separation, secret template) is well-structured. charts/agent-vault/templates/deployment.yaml is the most important file to revisit; charts/agent-vault/values.yaml needs a decision on a default network allowlist for the proxy.

Security Review

 - **SSRF via unrestricted MITM proxy** (`values.yaml` lines 81-83): The proxy service (port 14322) is a ClusterIP with no default `AGENT_VAULT_NETWORK_ALLOWLIST`. Any pod in the cluster with line-of-sight to that service can use it as a forward proxy to reach the Kubernetes API server, cloud instance-metadata endpoints (`169.254.169.254`), or other internal services not intended to be reachable by agent workloads. An opt-in comment is insufficient protection in a shared cluster.

AGENT_VAULT_NETWORK_ALLOWLIST left commented-out, leaving the MITM proxy without any network restriction by default. | | charts/agent-vault/templates/ingress.yaml | Standard ingress template; TLS secretName field is missing quote filter, unlike the host field. | | charts/agent-vault/templates/secret.yaml | Correctly conditional on existingSecret being unset; body:
Greptile Summary

 This PR adds opt-in response body redaction for services that may echo brokered credentials in upstream API responses. When enabled, the proxy materializes eligible text-like response bodies, replaces exact injected credential values with `[REDACTED]`, and fails closed with 502 for encoded, streaming, or oversized bodies. It also fixes a pre-existing bug where `inject` was not updated after a successful OAuth 401 retry. - **New `response_redaction.enabled` config**: opt-in per-service, propagated through proposal, merge, and inject pipelines with full validation and proposal-review display. - **`applyResponseRedactions` in forward.go**: materializes the response body, applies longest-first string replacement, strips stale integrity headers when the body is modified, and fail-closes with 502 on encoded, streaming, or oversized responses. - **`inject = retryInject` bug fix**: ensures the refreshed-token's redaction rules are applied to the retried response instead of the stale pre-retry rules.

Confidence Score: 3/5

The redaction and fail-closed logic is sound, but binary responses exceeding 64 MiB from a service with response_redaction enabled will be failed with 502 rather than passed through, contrary to the documented guarantee. The body is read into memory unconditionally before the content-type eligibility check runs. For most deployments this is invisible, but any service that also serves large binary assets with response_redaction enabled will have those large requests break with 502. internal/mitm/forward.go — specifically the applyResponseRedactions function and its interaction with the content-type eligibility check in brokercore.

Important Files Changed

| Filename | Overview | |----------|----------| | internal/mitm/forward.go | Adds response-redaction plumbing: body materialization, header cleanup, and fail-closed 502 paths. Fixes inject-not-updated on OAuth retry. Binary responses are materialized before the content-type eligibility check, causing large binary downloads to fail with 502 when redaction is enabled. | | internal/brokercore/response_redaction.go | New file: implements body redaction via longest-first string replacement, content-type eligibility check, and no-op pass-through for binary/empty bodies. | | internal/brokercore/credential.go | Adds Redactions field to InjectResult and populates it from raw credential values, rendered auth headers, and substitution values when ResponseRedactionEnabled. | | internal/proposal/merge.go | Extends metadata-only update path to carry ResponseRedaction alongside Enabled, and copies ResponseRedaction in toBrokerService. | | internal/mitm/response_redaction_test.go | New integration tests covering redaction of echoed secrets, disabled-by-default pass-through, fail-closed for encoded and oversized bodies. | Reviews (1): Last reviewed commit: ["add response body redaction"](https://github.com/infisical/agent-vault/commit/5dd536b5e30f1f6e7ebcfc9bdc5b7608173871fc) | [Re-trigger Greptile](https://app.greptile.com/api/retrigger?id=40706461)

# 🦉 What is GitGuardian?

GitGuardian Secrets Detection detects and fixes vulnerabilities in source code at every step of the software development lifecycle, covering 350+ types of secrets like API keys, database connection strings, private keys, certificates, and more. The platform’s policy engine enables security teams to monitor and enforce rules across their VCS, DevOps tools, and infrastructure-as-code configurations. Our automated remediation playbooks and collaboration features bring security and development teams together to resolve incidents fast and in full.

## 1. Scan your codebase for 350+ types of secrets
GitGuardian scans your GitHub repositories and raises alerts only for critical secrets, such as API keys or other credentials. At scale, GitGuardian’s detection algorithm has been battle-tested on over three years of activity in all public GitHub repositories – totaling over 1 billion scanned commits!

## 2. Quickly remediate your hard-coded secrets
If you ever experience a leak involving a credential, we have a complete remediation guide used by 100k+ developers each year. We’ll show you how to revoke the secret and remove it from your git history.

##  3. Prevent secrets from reaching GitHub
Install ggshield, the GitGuardian CLI, and add secrets detection to your local development workflow using pre-commit and pre-push git hooks integrations.

# 🙋‍♂️ FAQ

**What is your pricing?**
GitGuardian is free for teams under 25 developers and offers a 30-day trial for larger teams.

**How can I be sure that GitGuardian won’t raise too many false positives?**
We have scanned billions of commits, sent millions of alerts since 2018, and integrated each feedback to improve our algorithm. Our alerts currently receive 91% “true positive” feedback from developers.

**My repositories are private; why should I install automated secret detection?**
Imagine if there were a plain text file with all your credit card numbers inside, you wouldn’t put this file inside your company’s git repository. Secrets are just as sensitive and should be handled with special care.

**Is GitGuardian available to be installed on-premise?**
Yes, you can contact one of our security specialists to look over the possibility of installing GitGuardian on-premise on your repositories.

# ⚒️ Installation notes 

You should install GitGuardian directly through your [GitGuardian](https://dashboard.gitguardian.com/) workspace on the Integration settings page.

 Adds an optional `methods` list to broker services so the injected credential is attached only when the request's HTTP method matches. The check runs after service selection, parallel to `IsEnabled`, with no fall-through to a sibling on denial. Method-restricted services also have the well-known override surfaces (`X-HTTP-Method-Override`, `X-Method-Override`, `X-HTTP-Method` headers and `_method` query param) stripped before forwarding. - `broker.Service` gains `Methods []string`; `NormalizeAndValidateMethods` uppercases, deduplicates, and rejects unsupported or explicitly-empty lists; `AllowsMethod` does a case-sensitive comparison against the normalized list so non-uppercase input fails closed. - `CredentialProvider.Inject` gains a `method` parameter; `MethodNotAllowedError` wraps `ErrMethodNotAllowed` and carries the denied method and the allowed list for a structured 403 response. - `forwardRequest` strips `_method` from `outURL.RawQuery` (before `outReq` is built) and passes the override header names to `ApplyInjection` so they are not forwarded; the OAuth 401-retry path receives `r.Method` too, preserving the method check on refresh.

All Greptile review comments have been addressed and fixed (see commit ecea411 above) — SSRF protection added to the webhook client, Unicode-safe truncation, and the docs typo fixed.

This should be ready for a maintainer review whenever you get a chance. Would appreciate it if someone from the team could take a look and merge if it looks good. Thanks!

Thanks for the review, @greptile-apps! Addressed the unbounded database-backed scrapes issue in fb0ce55:

`/metrics` is unauthenticated (same as `/health`), so without a bound, a flood of concurrent scrapes could each open their own `CountProposalsByStatus` query and exhaust the database connection pool. The proposals collector now:

- Caches the result for 5s behind a mutex, so concurrent/rapid scrapes serialize on one in-flight query and share its result instead of each issuing their own.
- Caps the query itself with a 3s timeout, so a slow/hanging database can't pin a scrape (and a connection) indefinitely.
- Serves the last good cached value on a transient query failure instead of nothing, so a brief blip doesn't blank the gauge.

Added `TestProposalsCollector_CachesWithinTTL`, `TestProposalsCollector_ConcurrentScrapesShareOneQuery`, and `TestProposalsCollector_QueryTimesOutRatherThanBlockingForever` (all pass with `-race`) plus reran the full existing suite.

The implementation is clean and correct. The key design choices all hold up:

**Mutex-held-for-duration** (rather than a singleflight or separate "in-flight" flag) is the right call here — the 19 concurrent waiters serialise on one lock acquisition, each sees `cachedAt` within the TTL on their turn, and the store is hit exactly once. `TestProposalsCollector_ConcurrentScrapesShareOneQuery` proves this correctly: one goroutine acquires the lock and blocks on `release`; the other 19 wait on the mutex; after `close(counter.release)` the first completes and populates `c.cached`; each subsequent waiter finds a fresh cache hit and returns without calling the store.

**Stale-on-error** semantics (`return c.cached, c.cached != nil`) are exactly right — a transient blip shouldn't zero out the gauge on dashboards, and the `ok=false`-only-on-never-succeeded path matches the documented "skip on error" contract from before the cache was added.

**Timeout vs. TTL ordering** (`3s < 5s`) is sound — the query always gives up before the next scrape could legitimately bypass the cache.

One minor note: `TestProposalsCollector_QueryTimesOutRatherThanBlockingForever` waits up to `proposalsQueryTimeout + 2s = 5s` in the worst case, which will slow down the test suite on every run (not just failures). Since the test only needs to verify the query eventually unblocks, the outer deadline can be tighter — something like `proposalsQueryTimeout + 500*time.Millisecond` gives the same failure-detection guarantee without adding unnecessary wall-clock time on the happy path. Not a blocker, just worth tidying.

Everything else looks good — the concern is addressed.

Addressed the Greptile comment on the concurrent version allocation race (\`internal/store/sql_store.go\`):

- \`archiveCredentialVersionTx\`'s initial \`SELECT\` (which reads the current value before archiving it) now appends the dialect's \`FOR UPDATE\` clause, the same mechanism already used in \`CreateProposal\` for the analogous proposal-ID race. On Postgres this locks the \`credentials\` row for \`(vault_id, key)\` for the duration of the transaction, so two concurrent overwrites of the same credential (e.g. a manual \`credential set\` racing a proposal apply) are serialized instead of both computing the same \`MAX(version) + 1\` and one failing on the \`UNIQUE(vault_id, key, version)\` constraint. No-op on SQLite, which already serializes writers itself.

\`go build ./...\`, \`go vet ./...\`, and \`go test ./...\` all still pass (same pre-existing, unrelated \`internal/isolation\` failure as before, present on \`main\` too).

Greptile Summary

 This PR adds operator-managed OAuth providers to Agent Vault, starting with Google. The instance operator sets a shared client ID and secret via environment variables; each vault user then authorizes their own Google account and receives separately encrypted tokens, without ever seeing or supplying the shared credentials. - `internal/oauth/managed.go` loads provider config from env at startup, clears the secret from the process environment after reading it, and fails closed for partial config. - `internal/server/managed_oauth.go` and `handle_oauth.go` override the full provider config (URLs, client ID, secret, auth method) server-side before any further validation, so a user-supplied `authorization_url` or `token_url` in the request body is harmless when a managed provider is selected. - `handle_spa.go` exposes the list of configured provider IDs (no secrets) on the public `/v1/status` endpoint, which the frontend uses to render "Google (managed)" in the provider picker.

Confidence Score: 4/5

The core security invariant — that managed provider URLs and credentials are always overridden server-side before any token exchange — is correctly implemented and tested. The two findings are hardening gaps rather than exploitable flaws in the happy path. The managed provider override in applyManagedOAuthProvider is correct and the test suite covers the key security properties (URL override, unknown provider rejection). Two gaps exist: the DisablePKCE flag is not reset for managed providers, and only the client ID is whitespace-trimmed at load time. Neither causes data loss or token exfiltration, but both are worth addressing before shipping to operators. **Files Needing Attention:** internal/server/managed_oauth.go (DisablePKCE not enforced) and internal/oauth/managed.go (asymmetric trimming of client secret)

Hi @paulcdejean, apologies for the readme not being up to date. Agent Proxy is launching publicly soon (this Thursday), and that's when we'll make it more visible here.

We realized that the experience of managing secrets in Agent Vault is very limited, and hence users prefer to use a secrets management solution like Infisical to pull their secrets from. This is possible today by having your vault use Infisical as the credential store. However, you then have to manage your secrets on Infisical and your proxy settings on Agent Vault.

Agent Proxy is a more native offering, built inside Infisical itself, so everything stays in one place along with the rest of what Infisical gives you around your secrets.

@cjohnhanson , This PR’s method filtering gives agents an important distinction: a 403 can mean either “the upstream API rejected the request” or “Agent Vault policy denied it.”

Could we formalize broker-layer error responses as a stable, machine-readable contract? The existing X-Agent-Vault-Proxy-Error: true marker is useful as a lightweight source hint. Pairing it with application/problem+json (RFC 9457) would make clients simpler and avoid parsing human-readable messages.

For example, a denied method could return:

```http
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/problem+json
X-Agent-Vault-Proxy-Error: true

{
  "type": "https://agent-vault.dev/problems/method-not-allowed",
  "title": "Request method is not permitted by Agent Vault policy",
  "status": 403,
  "detail": "POST is not allowed for the matched service.",
  "code": "method_not_allowed",
  "allowed_methods": ["GET"]
}
```

Similar stable code/type values for service_not_found, service_disabled, credential_not_found, and proxy authentication failures would let an agent distinguish broker remediation from ordinary upstream API errors. Clients should use type/extensions—not detail—for behavior, and should still fail closed to a user approval workflow rather than automatically
widening access.

#351 bumped `@tailwindcss/vite` to 4.3.3, which pulled the lockfile's resolved `tailwindcss` up to **4.3.3** on `main`. The declared range there is `^4.3.0`, which already permits it, so this PR's change (`^4.3.0` → `^4.3.2`) would not alter the installed version — it now proposes a floor *below* what is already resolved.

The lockfile conflict here is against changes that made the bump redundant. If a range bump is still wanted, dependabot will raise a fresh one targeting 4.3.3.

OK, I won't notify you again about this release, but will get in touch when a new version is available. If you'd rather skip all updates until the next major or minor version, let me know by commenting `@dependabot ignore this major version` or `@dependabot ignore this minor version`. You can also ignore all major, minor, or patch releases for a dependency by adding an [`ignore` condition](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/supply-chain-security/configuration-options-for-dependency-updates#ignore) with the desired `update_types` to your config file.

If you change your mind, just re-open this PR and I'll resolve any conflicts on it.

reproduced this exactly - 3 bad-cred CONNECTs from one source IP exhaust the shared bucket and a different, valid credential from the same IP gets 429. confirmed the keying: mitmIPKey is r.RemoteAddr only, and both handleConnect (connect.go:56) and handleForward (forward.go:88) gate on it before Proxy-Authorization is even parsed, so the proxy can't tell tenants apart at that layer.

fix: key the flood gate on the presented credential instead - sha256 of the Proxy-Authorization value, so each credential gets its own budget and tokens never appear in rate-limit keys or logs. requests with no credential at all fall back to the peer IP, so pre-auth garbage floods are still gated. one bad actor behind a shared ingress can no longer 429 every other tenant behind it.

patch + regression test in the linked PR (test drives CONNECTs with two credentials through one source IP: pre-fix the second credential 429s, post-fix it doesn't, and the unauthenticated flood path still gates): https://github.com/Infisical/agent-vault/pull/406

Built by breken, your AI support engineer - breken.ai finds the bug, proves the fix with unmatched RCA, answers customers in your voice, and keeps your code and support docs clean - this one's on us.

Confidence Score: 3/5

The PR is not safe to merge until varying unauthenticated credential values can no longer bypass the authentication-failure flood gate.

Findings

1.   **Flood Gate Is Bypassable** ▶ 2.  **Forward Path Lacks Coverage** ▶

Summary

 - Separates failure budgets for different authorization headers sharing an ingress address. - Applies the new key to both CONNECT and HTTP forward requests. - Introduces an authentication-flood bypass because unauthenticated clients control the value used to select the bucket.
